author: Dylan Hahn
note: Clean figures (no title or notes) at fixed addresses, refreshed at every site update. Text fields describe the current data.

figures.title: Animation: development compared with every El Niño since 1950
figures.caption: Monthly Niño 3.4, Niño 1+2 and upper-ocean anomalies for every El Niño since 1950, aligned by onset year and drawn month by month; the box in each panel ranks the current event against all past events at the same stage.
figures.takeaway: At the latest month, 2026/2027 is warmer than every El Niño since 1950 at the same stage, both at the surface and in the upper ocean.
figures.how_to_read: Each line is one El Niño. The horizontal axis runs from January of the year the event began to December of the following year; the vertical axis shows how much warmer than normal the water was. A line above the others at a given month means that event was further developed at that point in the year.
figures.relation: Comparing every event at the same time of year shows whether 2026/2027 is an ordinary strong El Niño or is developing faster and further than past events, which helps judge how strong its peak may become.
figures.data: NOAA ERSST v5 (Niño 3.4 and Niño 1+2 sea surface temperature) and NCEP GODAS (upper-200 m temperature), anomalies from 1991–2020; El Niño events from NOAA CPC's Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI).
figures.description: Animated line charts in which every El Niño since 1950 advances month by month from January of its onset year. Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature: +2.9 °C in Sep, against a previous maximum of +2.2 °C at the same stage; Niño 1+2 sea surface temperature: +4.4 °C in Sep, against a previous maximum of +3.8 °C at the same stage; Upper-ocean (0–200 m) temperature: +4.6 °C in Sep, against a previous maximum of +3.2 °C at the same stage.

figures.title: Event development vs. past very strong events
figures.caption: Development of the 2026/2027 event in NOAA's Relative Oceanic Niño Index alongside the four strongest El Niño events since 1950, with NOAA's official forecast.
figures.takeaway: NOAA's official outlook places the peak of this event above the strongest El Niño since 1950.
figures.relation: RONI is the index NOAA uses to declare an El Niño and its strength. The forecast shows how strong the event is likely to be at its winter peak, when its effects on North American weather are greatest.
figures.data: NOAA CPC Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) and the official RONI outlook and strength probabilities.
figures.description: Line chart of El Niño strength from January 2026 to June 2027. 2026 rose from -0.9 °C in January to +1.7 °C now; NOAA's forecast peaks near +2.7 °C, above the record of +2.4 °C set in 1982/1983.

figures.title: Animation: sea surface temperature, 2026/2027 and past very strong events
figures.caption: Animated month-by-month sea surface temperature across the tropical Pacific (NOAA OISST, 0.25°), from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal, with the Niño 3.4 average for each.
figures.takeaway: Water warmer than 28 °C, normally confined to the western Pacific, now reaches farther east along the equator than in 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 or 1982/1983 at the same point in the year.
figures.how_to_read: Each map shows the actual sea surface temperature for one month. Red and dark red are warmer than about 28 °C (inside the black line), warm enough to fuel heavy tropical rainfall. Compare each year with the Normal panel at the bottom: during El Niño the warm area spreads east toward South America.
figures.relation: El Niño is defined by unusually warm water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. As the warm water spreads east, the rising air and heavy rain that normally sit over the western Pacific move east with it, which shifts weather patterns around the world.
figures.data: NOAA OISST v2.1 monthly mean sea surface temperature (0.25°), via NOAA PSL; normal = OISST 1991–2020 monthly mean.
figures.description: Animated maps of tropical Pacific sea surface temperature from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027 (to September 2026), 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal. In September of the first year, the Niño 3.4 region averaged 29.7 °C in 2026/2027, 28.3 °C in 2023/2024, 28.5 °C in 2015/2016, 28.6 °C in 1997/1998, 28.0 °C in 1982/1983, and 26.7 °C normally.

figures.title: Sea surface temperature by event
figures.caption: Tropical Pacific sea surface temperature in the same month of 2026 and of each past strong El Niño year, with Niño 3.4 and tropical-mean anomalies.
figures.takeaway: In the same month, 2026/2027 is warmer than past very strong events both in the Niño 3.4 region and across the tropical Pacific as a whole.
figures.relation: Comparing the same month of each strong El Niño shows how far the warm water has spread in 2026/2027, and that the whole tropical ocean is warmer than in past events, which adds to El Niño's effect on global temperature.
figures.data: Maps: NOAA ERSST v5 monthly sea surface temperature (2°). Anomaly values: NOAAGlobalTemp v6, relative to 1991–2020.
figures.description: 5 maps of tropical Pacific surface temperature in August of 2026, 2023, 2015, 1997, 1982. 2026: Niño 3.4 +2.1 °C, whole tropics +0.8 °C; 2023: Niño 3.4 +1.3 °C, whole tropics +0.7 °C; 2015: Niño 3.4 +1.7 °C, whole tropics +0.4 °C; 1997: Niño 3.4 +1.7 °C, whole tropics +0.1 °C; 1982: Niño 3.4 +0.5 °C, whole tropics -0.3 °C.

figures.title: Warming across the Niño regions
figures.caption: Location of the four Niño regions and their monthly anomalies, showing where along the equator the warming is concentrated.
figures.takeaway: Warming is strongest near South America and weakest in the western Pacific, a pattern closest to 1997/1998.
figures.how_to_read: The map shows the four standard boxes along the equator, from Niño 4 in the west to Niño 1+2 off South America. Each chart plots how much warmer than normal one box has been, month by month.
figures.relation: Where the warming is strongest matters: El Niños that peak near South America and those that peak in the central Pacific affect weather in different ways.
figures.data: NOAA CPC monthly Niño region indices (from OISST v2.1), anomalies from 1991–2020.
figures.description: Line charts of monthly SST anomalies in the Niño 4, 3.4, 3 and 1+2 regions for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983. In September 2026: Niño 4 +0.9 °C; Niño 3.4 +2.8 °C; Niño 3 +3.6 °C; Niño 1+2 +4.7 °C. Closest past event at the same stage: 1997/1998.

figures.title: Eastern Pacific or Central Pacific El Niño?
figures.caption: Two indices that separate warming near South America (Eastern Pacific type) from warming near the date line (Central Pacific type), for 2026/2027 and four past strong events, and every El Niño since 1950 at its peak.
figures.takeaway: So far 2026/2027 is a clear Eastern Pacific El Niño, like 1997/1998 and 1982/1983: the warming is centred near South America, while the central Pacific is close to normal.
figures.how_to_read: Orange shows warming near South America, blue warming near the date line. In the lower chart each dot is one El Niño at its peak: dots high and to the left warmed mostly in the east; dots below the dashed line warmed mostly in the central Pacific.
figures.relation: El Niños centred near South America and those centred near the date line shift the atmosphere's heating to different places, so they affect rainfall and temperature around the world, including California, differently. The strongest past El Niños for California rainfall, 1982/1983 and 1997/1998, were Eastern Pacific events.
figures.data: NOAA ERSST v5 Niño 3 (5°S–5°N, 150°W–90°W) and Niño 4 (5°S–5°N, 160°E–150°W) anomalies from 1991–2020, combined as in Ren and Jin (2011): Eastern Pacific = Niño 3 − 0.4 × Niño 4, Central Pacific = Niño 4 − 0.4 × Niño 3 when both have the same sign; 3-month means.
figures.description: Line charts of the Eastern Pacific and Central Pacific El Niño indices for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983, and a scatter plot of every El Niño since 1950 at its peak. Over September 2026 and the two months before, the 2026/2027 event had an Eastern Pacific index of +2.5 °C and a Central Pacific index of -0.1 °C (Eastern Pacific type); at their peaks, 2023/2024 +1.4 and +0.7 °C, 2015/2016 +2.1 and +0.2 °C, 1997/1998 +2.9 and -0.6 °C and 1982/1983 +2.4 and -0.6 °C.

figures.title: Equatorial SST evolution (Hovmöller)
figures.caption: Sea surface temperature along the equator, month by month (rows, top to bottom) and from the western Pacific to South America (left to right), for 2026/2027 and four past strong events.
figures.takeaway: Surface warming in the eastern Pacific is stronger in 2026/2027 than at the same time in any past very strong event.
figures.how_to_read: Time runs down the page, one row per month; position runs left to right from the western Pacific to South America. Red marks warmer-than-normal water. Warmth that slants down and to the right is moving east over time.
figures.relation: Following the surface temperature month by month shows how El Niño spread east across the Pacific and how quickly the eastern Pacific warmed compared with past events.
figures.data: NOAA ERSST v5 monthly sea surface temperature (2°) along 2°S–2°N; anomalies from 1991–2020.
figures.description: Longitude–time diagrams of sea surface temperature anomalies along the equatorial Pacific for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983. Maximum eastern Pacific anomaly in September: 2026 +4.7 °C; 2023 +2.9 °C; 2015 +3.0 °C; 1997 +3.7 °C; 1982 +2.5 °C.

figures.title: Animation: the tropical Pacific in 3D
figures.caption: Rotating 3D view of the tropical Pacific in a normal year and in 2026/2027: the top surface is the temperature at 5 m and the lower surface the base of the warm layer (the 20 °C isotherm), from January 2026 to the latest month.
figures.takeaway: In a normal year the warm layer is thin near South America; in 2026/2027 it has thickened there, so the cold water that normally cools the eastern Pacific stays far below the surface.
figures.how_to_read: Each block is the tropical Pacific seen from the south-east, with Asia at the far left and South America at the right. The coloured lower surface is the base of the warm layer: red where it lies deep, blue where it is close to the surface. The thin top sheet is the sea surface temperature.
figures.relation: The trade winds normally hold the warm layer deep in the west and shallow in the east. When the winds weaken during El Niño, the warm layer flattens, so cold water no longer reaches the surface near South America and the eastern Pacific warms from below.
figures.data: NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature in 10 m levels to 205 m, via NOAA PSL; normal = 1991–2020 mean temperature.
figures.description: Rotating 3D animation of the tropical Pacific comparing a normal year with 2026 from January 2026 to September 2026. In September, the base of the warm layer on the equator east of 130°W lay at about 130 m in 2026, against 51 m normally.

figures.title: Warm water stored before each El Niño began
figures.caption: NOAA PMEL's equatorial warm water volume in the six months before every El Niño since 1980 began, and month by month from 18 months before to 12 months after.
figures.takeaway: 2026/2027 began with more warm water stored along the equator than most El Niños, and the store has kept growing since, to more than any past El Niño at the same stage.
figures.how_to_read: Top: one bar per El Niño since 1980, showing how much more warm water than normal was stored in the six months before it began. Bottom: the same measure month by month, with every event lined up on the month it began (dashed line). Warm water normally drains away once an El Niño is under way.
figures.relation: Warm water must build up along the equator before an El Niño can grow (the "recharge"), and El Niño then drains it toward higher latitudes (the "discharge"). A large store before and during an event provides the heat that sustains warming at the surface.
figures.data: NOAA PMEL warm water volume (above the 20 °C isotherm, 5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W), monthly from 1980; anomalies from 1991–2020. Event start: the first month of each El Niño in NOAA CPC's RONI (+0.5 °C or more).
figures.description: Bar chart and line chart of equatorial Pacific warm water volume before and during every El Niño since 1980. Average anomaly in the six months before each event began: 2026/2027 +1.6, 2023/2024 +2.2, 2015/2016 +0.9, 1997/1998 +1.7 and 1982/1983 +1.4 × 10¹⁴ m³; average of all past events +0.7.

figures.title: Animation: warm water moving across the Pacific
figures.caption: Animated maps of the depth of the 20 °C isotherm (the thickness of the warm upper layer) from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal, with the equatorial warm water volume (5°S–5°N) and its departure from normal.
figures.takeaway: More warm water is stored along the equator in 2026/2027 than at the same stage of 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 or 1982/1983.
figures.how_to_read: Each map shows how far below the surface the warm upper layer reaches (the depth of the 20 °C isotherm). Dark red means warm water extends deep; blue means the warm layer is thin. Watch the band between the dashed lines: during El Niño the red area spreads east along the equator.
figures.relation: Warm water volume is one of the earliest signs of El Niño: it builds up along the equator in the months before an event and is drained away from the equator as the event peaks and fades.
figures.data: NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature to 205 m, via NOAA PSL; warm water volume as defined by NOAA PMEL (above 20 °C, 5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W).
figures.description: Animated maps of the depth of the 20 °C isotherm across the tropical Pacific from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983 (the current event to September 2026) and the 1991–2020 normal. In September of the first year, the equatorial warm water volume departed from normal by +3.0 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 2026/2027, +0.8 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 2023/2024, +1.0 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 2015/2016, +1.6 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 1997/1998 and +2.5 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 1982/1983.

figures.title: Animation: layers of warm water
figures.caption: Equatorial sections coloured by temperature layer (20–24, 24–26, 26–28, 28–29 and above 29 °C) for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal, with the volume of water in each layer between 5°S and 5°N, from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next.
figures.takeaway: The hottest water has grown the most: the volume warmer than 28 °C is far above normal and above 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983 at the same stage.
figures.how_to_read: Each slice runs along the equator from Asia (left) to South America (right) and from 5 m down to 200 m. Colours mark temperature layers, from below 20 °C (dark blue) to above 29 °C (dark red); compare each year with the Normal panel at the bottom to see how much deeper and farther east the warm layers reach. The bar beside each slice adds up the volume in each layer, warmest on the left.
figures.relation: Water above about 28 °C fuels the deep thunderstorms of the tropics. The more of it there is and the farther east it reaches, the farther the tropical rainfall belt shifts, which drives El Niño's effects on weather elsewhere.
figures.data: NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature to 205 m, via NOAA PSL; sections 2°S–2°N, volumes 5°S–5°N, 120°E–80°W; normal = 1991–2020 mean temperature.
figures.description: Animated equatorial Pacific sections coloured by temperature layer from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and Normal (1991–2020) (the current event to September 2026), with bars of warm water volume by layer. In September of the first year, water above 28 °C between 5°S and 5°N totalled 13.7 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 2026/2027, 10.6 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 2023/2024, 10.3 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 2015/2016, 10.2 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 1997/1998, 8.2 × 10¹⁴ m³ in 1982/1983 and 7.3 × 10¹⁴ m³ in Normal (1991–2020); water above 20 °C totalled 26.7, 24.6, 24.7, 25.4, 26.2 and 23.7 × 10¹⁴ m³ respectively.

figures.title: Animation: upper-ocean temperature, 2026/2027 and past very strong events
figures.caption: Animated equatorial upper-ocean temperature sections for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998, 1982/1983 and the 1991–2020 normal; during El Niño the warm layer deepens in the east and the 20 °C line flattens.
figures.takeaway: In 2026/2027 the 20 °C line is nearly flat across the Pacific: the cold water that normally lies close to the surface in the east has been pushed down.
figures.how_to_read: Each panel is a vertical slice through the ocean along the equator, from Asia (left) to South America (right) and from the surface (top) to 200 m depth (bottom). Warm colours above the black line are the warm upper layer. Normally the line rises toward the east; during El Niño it flattens.
figures.relation: The tilt of the warm layer along the equator is the clearest sign of El Niño below the surface: when it flattens, cold water no longer reaches the surface near South America, so the eastern Pacific warms.
figures.data: NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature to 205 m averaged over 2°S–2°N, via NOAA PSL; normal = 1991–2020.
figures.description: Animated depth–longitude sections of equatorial Pacific ocean temperature from January of each El Niño's first year to December of the next, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983 (the current event to September 2026) and the 1991–2020 normal. In September of the first year, the upper 200 m east of 180° departed from normal by +4.6 °C in 2026/2027, +1.3 °C in 2023/2024, +2.3 °C in 2015/2016, +3.2 °C in 1997/1998 and +2.5 °C in 1982/1983.

figures.title: Upper-ocean temperature by event
figures.caption: Equatorial upper-ocean temperature at the same stage of each event; the current event holds substantially more subsurface heat.
figures.takeaway: The upper ocean holds far more extra heat in 2026/2027 than in any past very strong event at the same stage.
figures.how_to_read: Each panel is a vertical slice along the equator, from Asia (left) to South America (right), down to 200 m. Colours show how much warmer (red) or cooler (blue) than normal the water is.
figures.relation: Heat stored below the surface tends to reach the surface over the following months, so more subsurface heat than in past events at the same stage points to continued warming.
figures.data: NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly temperature to 205 m averaged over 2°S–2°N, via NOAA PSL; anomalies from 1991–2020.
figures.description: Depth-by-longitude slices of the equatorial Pacific in September of 2026, 2023, 2015, 1997, 1982. Average extra warmth in the top 200 m from 180° to 80°W: 2026: +4.6 °C; 2023: +1.3 °C; 2015: +2.3 °C; 1997: +3.2 °C; 1982: +2.5 °C.

figures.title: Upper-ocean heat content (Hovmöller)
figures.caption: Average temperature of the upper 200 m along the equator, month by month (rows, top to bottom) and from the western Pacific to South America (left to right), for 2026/2027 and four past strong events; warm water spreading east beneath the surface marks Kelvin waves.
figures.takeaway: Warm water spreading east beneath the surface has built a larger heat reservoir in 2026/2027 than in past very strong events.
figures.how_to_read: Time runs down the page, one row per month; position runs left to right from the western Pacific to South America. Colours show the average temperature anomaly of the top 200 m. Diagonal streaks running down and to the right are Kelvin waves: pulses of warm water that cross the Pacific beneath the surface in about two months.
figures.relation: Following the upper-ocean heat month by month shows the Kelvin waves that carried warm water east, and the build-up below the surface that came before the surface warming.
figures.data: NCEP GODAS ocean reanalysis, monthly mean temperature of the top 200 m over 2°S–2°N, via NOAA PSL; anomalies from 1991–2020.
figures.description: Longitude–time diagrams of upper-200 m temperature anomalies along the equatorial Pacific for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016, 1997/1998 and 1982/1983. Central–eastern Pacific mean in September: 2026 +4.6 °C; 2023 +1.3 °C; 2015 +2.3 °C; 1997 +3.2 °C; 1982 +2.5 °C.

figures.title: Westerly wind bursts along the equator (Hovmöller)
figures.caption: Daily surface wind along the equator compared with normal, from October of the year before each El Niño to January after its first year, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016 and 1997/1998: red streaks are westerly wind bursts.
figures.takeaway: From June to September 2026 the wind over the central Pacific was more westerly than normal on almost every day, by 4.5 m/s on average: a larger weakening of the trade winds than in 1997 (3.8 m/s), 2015 (2.9 m/s) or 2023 (0.4 m/s) over the same months.
figures.how_to_read: Time runs down the page, one row per day, from October of the year before each El Niño; position runs left to right from the western Pacific to South America. Red streaks are westerly wind bursts: spells of wind blowing toward South America, against the usual trade winds. Each strong burst is followed by a Kelvin wave in the figures below.
figures.relation: The trade winds normally pile warm water up in the western Pacific. Westerly wind bursts briefly reverse them, sending pulses of warm water east as Kelvin waves; repeated bursts, and the weakening of the trade winds as the ocean warms, are what turn a developing El Niño into a strong one.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI Blended Sea Winds v2, daily 10 m zonal wind (0.25°), averaged over 5°S–5°N; anomalies from the NCEI 1991–2020 monthly climatology; 5-day running means. Days missing from NCEI's record (all of May 2026) are filled with CCMP v2.1 near-real-time winds (Remote Sensing Systems), adjusted to match NCEI.
figures.description: Longitude–time diagrams of daily equatorial east–west wind anomalies from October of the year before to January after the first year of the El Niños of 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016 and 1997/1998. Westerly wind bursts from October to 30 September: 2026/2027 7, 2023/2024 6, 2015/2016 10 and 1997/1998 6.

figures.title: Animation: Kelvin waves
figures.caption: Every Kelvin wave since October 2025 traced in daily satellite sea level along the equator: each pulse raises sea level by a few centimetres as it crosses the Pacific.
figures.takeaway: A series of Kelvin waves has carried warm water from the western Pacific to South America since late 2025, each one adding to the warm layer in the east.
figures.how_to_read: Top: sea level height (SSH) along the equator on the day shown, rising in the east as warm water piles up. Bottom: the Kelvin-wave signal day by day, with time running down the page, so each wave is a red streak slanting down to the right. White dashed lines trace each wave once it has crossed the Pacific. Use the cm and inches buttons above the figure to switch units.
figures.relation: Kelvin waves carry warm water from the western to the eastern Pacific. Each one deepens the warm layer in the east and warms the surface there one to two months later, which helps forecasters anticipate further warming.
figures.data: NOAA blended satellite altimetry, daily sea surface height anomaly (0.25°), averaged over 1°S–1°N, via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP; anomalies from the 2017–2024 seasonal cycle.
figures.description: Animated infographic of Kelvin waves along the equatorial Pacific from October 2025 to 27 October 2026, from daily satellite sea level. 6 Kelvin waves crossed the Pacific: wave 1 left 150°E on 23 November and reached 95°W on 29 January 2026 at 2.2 m/s; wave 2 left 150°E on 14 January and reached 95°W on 7 March 2026 at 2.8 m/s; wave 3 left 150°E on 14 March and reached 95°W on 5 May 2026 at 2.8 m/s; wave 4 left 150°E on 3 April and reached 95°W on 18 May 2026 at 3.3 m/s; wave 5 left 150°E on 2 July and reached 95°W on 21 August 2026 at 3.0 m/s; wave 6 left 150°E on 24 August and reached 95°W on 15 October 2026 at 2.8 m/s. Sea level east of 130°W rose from -5 cm to +47 cm over the period.

figures.title: How fast the Kelvin waves crossed the Pacific
figures.caption: The speed of every Kelvin wave traced in satellite sea level since 2017, and the days each took to cross from 150°E to 95°W, against the ENSO state at the time.
figures.takeaway: The 2026 Kelvin waves were not unusually fast: they crossed at a median of 2.8 m/s, about 53 days from 150°E to 95°W, the same as the median of all clear waves since 2017.
figures.how_to_read: Each dot is one Kelvin wave, placed at the date it was halfway across and at its speed; the right-hand axis gives the same speed as days to cross. Bigger dots raised sea level more; the bars show how precisely each speed is known. The grey band is the speed theory predicts for the fastest type of Kelvin wave; red and blue shading mark El Niño and La Niña.
figures.relation: The speed of a Kelvin wave sets how long the warm water takes to reach South America, and so how much warning the ocean gives before the eastern Pacific warms. Speed depends on how the ocean is layered: a thicker warm layer and eastward currents make waves faster.
figures.data: NOAA blended near-real-time altimetry (sea surface height anomaly, 0.25°, daily, from 2017), 1°S–1°N, via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP; ENSO state from NOAA CPC's RONI.
figures.description: Scatter chart of the speed of every Kelvin wave traced along the equatorial Pacific since 2017. The 6 waves of the 2026/2027 El Niño travelled at 2.2, 2.8, 2.8, 3.3, 3.0 and 2.8 m/s, median 2.8 m/s; other clear waves since 2017 had a median of 2.8 m/s.

figures.title: Coastal sea level from Ecuador to Washington
figures.caption: Daily tide-gauge sea level along the Pacific coast of the Americas, from Peru and Ecuador to Neah Bay, Washington, for 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016 and 1997/1998.
figures.takeaway: By August 2026 coastal sea level had risen about 25 cm in Ecuador and 14 cm at San Diego, but not yet in Oregon and Washington; in 1997 the northern coast rose from the middle of the year.
figures.how_to_read: Each row is one tide gauge, from Peru at the bottom to Washington at the top (numbered on the map); time runs from left to right. Red is higher sea level than normal. A rise that appears first in the lower rows and later in the upper rows is a wave travelling north along the coast. Grey rows had no working gauge at the time.
figures.relation: Coastal-trapped Kelvin waves carry El Niño's warm water poleward along the coasts of the Americas, raising sea level and warming coastal waters as far as California and the Pacific Northwest. Higher coastal sea level adds to flooding and erosion during winter storms and high tides.
figures.data: University of Hawaii Sea Level Center fast-delivery daily tide-gauge data; anomalies from each station's 1991–2020 seasonal cycle, 10-day means, not corrected for air pressure.
figures.description: Time–distance diagrams of coastal sea level anomalies at tide gauges from Peru to Washington for the El Niños of 2026/2027, 2023/2024, 2015/2016 and 1997/1998. In August 2026: La Libertad, Ecuador +25 cm, San Diego, CA +14 cm and Neah Bay, WA +2 cm; in August 1997: La Libertad, Ecuador +8 cm, San Diego, CA +6 cm and Neah Bay, WA +13 cm.

figures.title: Animation: coastal sea level, day by day
figures.caption: Daily tide-gauge sea level along the coast from Ecuador to Washington since October 2025, built up day by day: a rise that travels north shows as a streak slanting down to the right.
figures.takeaway: Sea level along the coast rose first near the equator, in Ecuador and Costa Rica from May 2026, and later and less in California; Oregon and Washington have barely risen so far.
figures.how_to_read: Top: sea level at each tide gauge on the day shown, from Ecuador (left) to Washington (right). Bottom: the same day by day, with time running down the page, so a rise that travels north along the coast is a streak slanting down to the right. The map colours each gauge by its sea level on the day shown; the numbers match the columns.
figures.relation: Coastal-trapped Kelvin waves carry El Niño's warm water poleward along the coasts of the Americas. Watching the rise move from gauge to gauge shows how far north the waves have reached and how quickly.
figures.data: University of Hawaii Sea Level Center fast-delivery daily tide-gauge data; anomalies from each station's 1991–2020 seasonal cycle, 10-day means, not corrected for air pressure.
figures.description: Animated chart of coastal sea level at 7 tide gauges from Peru to Washington, from October 2025 to 31 August 2026. Over the last 30 days of data: La Libertad, Ecuador +26 cm, San Diego, CA +15 cm and Neah Bay, WA +2 cm compared with normal.

figures.title: Ranking of El Niño events since 1950
figures.caption: El Niño events since 1950 ranked by peak strength, duration and accumulated intensity, with the current event completed by NOAA's median forecast.
figures.takeaway: If NOAA's median forecast is realised, 2026/2027 would rank first by peak strength among El Niño events since 1950.
figures.relation: Peak strength, length and total warmth each relate to impacts: stronger and longer events tend to have larger and more dependable effects on weather worldwide, including California's winter rainfall.
figures.data: NOAA CPC Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), 1950–present, completed for the current event with NOAA's official median outlook.
figures.description: Ranked bar charts of the 12 strongest El Niños since 1950 by peak strength, length in months and total extra warmth. 2026/2027: peak +2.7 °C, 10 months (forecast); 1982/1983: peak +2.4 °C, 13 months; 1997/1998: peak +2.3 °C, 12 months; 2015/2016: peak +2.2 °C, 14 months; 1991/1992: peak +2.1 °C, 15 months; 1965/1966: peak +2.0 °C, 12 months; 1972/1973: peak +2.0 °C, 12 months; 1957/1958: peak +1.9 °C, 16 months; 2009/2010: peak +1.5 °C, 7 months; 1986/1987: peak +1.5 °C, 17 months; 2023/2024: peak +1.4 °C, 8 months; 2002/2003: peak +1.3 °C, 7 months.

figures.title: Verification of NOAA's 2026 forecasts
figures.caption: Each monthly NOAA strength forecast issued since April 2026 compared with the observed RONI, and how confidence in a very strong peak has evolved.
figures.takeaway: NOAA's confidence in a very strong peak has risen with every forecast issued since April 2026.
figures.relation: Knowing how NOAA's forecasts for this event have performed shows how much confidence to place in the current outlook for its peak.
figures.data: NOAA CPC official ENSO strength probabilities (monthly archive since April 2026) and the observed Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI).
figures.description: Verification of NOAA's 2026 El Niño strength forecasts. For Jul–Sep 2026 (observed +1.69 °C, strong), forecasts by issue month gave the observed category: April 11%; May 17%; June 36%; July 57%; August 76%. Probability of a very strong peak in Nov 2026–Jan 2027 by issue: April 25%; May 37%; June 63%; July 75%; August 90%; September 93%; October 96%.

figures.title: Global temperature and El Niño
figures.caption: Annual global mean surface temperature anomalies; recent record years have coincided with El Niño events.
figures.takeaway: Many of the record-warm years since 1950 coincided with El Niño, which temporarily adds to the long-term warming.
figures.relation: El Niño releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, temporarily raising global average temperature on top of long-term warming; the year during or after a strong El Niño is often a new record.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI global land and ocean surface temperature (NOAAGlobalTemp), relative to 1901–2000; El Niño winters from NOAA CPC RONI (December–February).
figures.description: Bar chart of global temperature each year since 1950, rising over time. Highlighted record years that came with an El Niño winter: 1995, 1998, 2010, 2016, 2024. 2026 so far is +1.15 °C above the 20th-century average.

figures.title: Summer 2026 temperature anomalies
figures.caption: June–September 2026 daytime-high and overnight-low anomalies across Southern California (NOAA nClimGrid, ~5 km), and the regional overnight-low anomaly for every summer since 1950.
figures.takeaway: Summer 2026 nights were among the warmest on record across the region; daytime highs were less exceptional.
figures.relation: El Niño's main influence on Southern California comes in winter. This summer's heat coincided with the developing event and record-warm coastal water, so these maps put summer 2026 in context.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI nClimGrid monthly (~5 km) mean daily maximum and minimum temperature, June–September, land only; anomalies from 1991–2020.
figures.description: Maps of Southern California June–September 2026 temperature anomalies relative to 1991–2020: daytime highs +0.7 °C (7th warmest since 1950), overnight lows +1.7 °C (2nd warmest). Bar chart of the regional overnight-low anomaly for every summer since 1950.

figures.title: Warm nights and hot days by station
figures.caption: Station counts of warm nights (≥ 65 °F) and hot days (≥ 90 °F) each summer since 1950 at Los Angeles, San Diego, the Inland Empire and Santa Barbara.
figures.takeaway: Warm nights were far more frequent than usual in summer 2026 at every station, and Santa Barbara set a record.
figures.relation: Warm coastal water keeps nights warmer near the coast, and El Niño years can bring warm water to Southern California; the station records show how this summer compares with past El Niño and other years.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily station records (Los Angeles, San Diego, Inland Empire, Santa Barbara), June–September; El Niño strength from NOAA CPC RONI.
figures.description: Bar charts of warm nights and hot days each summer since 1950 at Los Angeles, San Diego, the Inland Empire and Santa Barbara. Summer 2026: Los Angeles 64 warm nights (12th of 77, typical 40); San Diego 86 warm nights (9th of 77, typical 55); Inland Empire 55 warm nights (2nd of 35, typical 26); Santa Barbara 44 warm nights (1st of 70, typical 4).

figures.title: Marine heat in the Southern California Bight
figures.caption: Daily sea surface temperature and marine heatwave days in the Southern California Bight since 1982 (NOAA OISST), with 2026 compared with 1997 and 2015.
figures.takeaway: Coastal waters off Southern California have had more marine heatwave days in 2026 than in any previous year by the same date.
figures.how_to_read: A marine heatwave day is part of a spell of at least five days when the water is warmer than 90% of past values for that time of year. Each year is compared through the same calendar date.
figures.relation: El Niño can warm the waters off California, through ocean waves travelling up the coast and changes in the winds. Marine heatwaves affect fisheries, kelp forests and coastal temperatures.
figures.data: NOAA OISST v2.1 daily sea surface temperature (0.25°), via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP, averaged over the Southern California Bight; marine heatwaves after Hobday et al. (2016).
figures.description: Marine heatwave days and sea surface temperature anomalies in the Southern California Bight since 1982. By 2 October 2026: 229 heatwave days; same date in 1997: 20, 2015: 165. Recent 30-day mean anomaly +2.8 °C.

figures.title: Animation: marine heatwaves from California to Peru
figures.caption: Daily marine heatwave category (I Moderate to IV Extreme) across the eastern Pacific from 25°S to 45°N since January 2026 (NOAA OISST), with the share of the coastal waters off Southern California and off Ecuador and Peru in each category.
figures.takeaway: On 20 October 2026 the whole coastal ocean off Ecuador and Peru was in a marine heatwave, 70% of it Severe or Extreme, and half the coastal waters off Southern California and northern Baja were in a Strong or Severe heatwave.
figures.how_to_read: Colours show the category of marine heatwave on each day: the more times the water exceeds its usual range for that time of year, the higher the category. Light grey-blue is ocean with no heatwave. The charts on the right show how much of each coastal box (A and B on the map) was in each category as the year went on.
figures.relation: El Niño warms the coastal ocean of the Americas through coastal Kelvin waves and weaker winds. Prolonged marine heatwaves stress fisheries, kelp forests and coral, and can bring toxic algal blooms and unusual marine species to Southern California.
figures.data: NOAA OISST v2.1 daily sea surface temperature (0.25°, used every 1°), via NOAA PSL; marine heatwaves and categories after Hobday et al. (2016, 2018), with a 1991–2020 baseline.
figures.description: Animated map of marine heatwave categories from January 2026 to 20 October 2026 over the eastern Pacific from 25°S to 45°N, with charts of the share of two coastal regions in each category. On 20 October 2026: Southern California and northern Baja 77% in a heatwave, at most III Severe and Ecuador and Peru (Niño 1+2) 100% in a heatwave, at most IV Extreme.

figures.title: Long-term increase in summer heat
figures.caption: Change in summer daytime highs and overnight lows since 1951–1980 across Southern California, and the regional summer temperature record since 1895 (NOAA nClimGrid).
figures.takeaway: Summer nights across Southern California have warmed more than summer days since the mid-20th century.
figures.relation: Long-term warming sets the baseline: any heat related to El Niño now comes on top of summers that are already warmer than in the past.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI nClimGrid monthly (~5 km) June–September mean daily maximum and minimum temperature since 1895; El Niño winters from NOAA CPC RONI.
figures.description: Maps and time series of Southern California summer temperature since 1895. Change from 1951–1980 to 1996–2025: daytime highs +1.1 °C, overnight lows +1.3 °C. Five hottest summers: 2018, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024.

figures.title: NOAA seasonal precipitation outlook
figures.caption: NOAA Climate Prediction Center probability of above-, near- or below-normal precipitation for Southern California, with season-by-season values for Los Angeles.
figures.takeaway: NOAA's outlook favours a wetter-than-normal winter in Southern California, most strongly from December onward.
figures.relation: During El Niño the Pacific jet stream tends to shift south in winter, steering more storms toward Southern California; NOAA's seasonal outlook reflects this.
figures.data: NOAA Climate Prediction Center official 3-month precipitation outlooks (GIS files).
figures.description: Map of NOAA's Dec–Feb precipitation outlook for Southern California, issued October 15, 2026. Los Angeles by season: Nov–Jan: 40–50% chance wetter; Dec–Feb: 50–60% chance wetter; Jan–Mar: 60–70% chance wetter; Feb–Apr: 50–60% chance wetter; Mar–May: 40–50% chance wetter.

figures.title: Precipitation in strong El Niño winters
figures.caption: November–March precipitation across Southern California during the strong El Niño winters since 1951 (NOAA nClimGrid, ~5 km), and the regional total for every winter.
figures.takeaway: Most strong El Niño winters, though not all, have been wetter than normal across Southern California.
figures.relation: This shows how often strong El Niño winters have actually brought more rain to Southern California, and that some, such as 2015/2016, did not.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI nClimGrid monthly precipitation (~5 km), November–March totals; El Niño strength from NOAA CPC RONI (December–February).
figures.description: Maps of Southern California November–March precipitation during 7 strong El Niño winters (1957/1958, 1965/1966, 1972/1973, 1982/1983, 1991/1992, 1997/1998, 2015/2016): regional mean 146% of normal, 6 of 7 winters wetter than normal. Bar chart of every winter since 1951 coloured by ENSO phase.

figures.title: Station precipitation by ENSO phase
figures.caption: Water-year precipitation by ENSO phase at Los Angeles, San Diego, Lake Elsinore and Santa Barbara, 1951 to present.
figures.takeaway: Strong El Niño seasons have usually been wet in Los Angeles and San Diego; the signal is weaker inland and farther north.
figures.relation: Long station records show how rainfall at individual places has varied with El Niño and La Niña, including how dependable the El Niño signal is in each part of the region.
figures.data: NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily station records (water years October–September); El Niño strength from NOAA CPC RONI (December–February).
figures.description: Bar chart of every Los Angeles rainy season since 1951 as a percent of normal, coloured by El Niño or La Niña strength, and dot plots for Los Angeles, San Diego, the Inland Empire and Santa Barbara. Los Angeles: 6 of 7 strong El Niño seasons wetter than normal, median 147%; San Diego: 6 of 7 strong El Niño seasons wetter than normal, median 145%; Inland Empire: 4 of 6 strong El Niño seasons wetter than normal, median 113%; Santa Barbara: 3 of 5 strong El Niño seasons wetter than normal, median 104%.
